Rotation vs reflection: turning or flipping a shape?

Use an asymmetric shape to tell a rotation from a mirror reflection, one movement at a time.

By Biel Sardà · Published 1 Oct 2026 · Suggest a correction

Try it with a paper shape

Cut an L shape from paper. Turn it a quarter-turn on the table. Its size and outline stay the same, but it points a different way. This is a rotation.

Now imagine looking at it in a mirror. The bend changes sides. That is a reflection. A shape with a clearly marked corner makes the difference easier to notice than a plain circle would.

Try it yourself

Draw an L on paper and mark one corner with a dot. Turn the paper a quarter-turn on the table. Four quarter-turns return it to its starting position. Then hold it beside a mirror to compare a reflection.

Follow the small dot as well as the outside edge. The dot is attached to the shape, so it moves with it. This prevents a symmetric-looking outline from hiding what changed.

Use the direction in the question

A clockwise quarter-turn follows the direction of clock hands. A half-turn rotates through two quarter-turns. A full turn is four quarter-turns, or 360 degrees.

A reflection needs a mirror line. With a vertical mirror line, left and right switch. A horizontal mirror would switch top and bottom instead.

Check features, not a vague impression

Look for a short arm, a long arm and a marked corner. Track where each feature moves. If only one feature matches your prediction, you may have turned the shape the wrong way or imagined a reflection.

Some shapes, such as a square without a mark, can look unchanged after certain movements. That does not mean no movement happened. Distinctive features make a reasoning question less ambiguous.
